name: Hogan's Store
aka: the log store at Lake and South Water

documented_range.note: THE START IS THE FIRST DATE A SOURCE PUTS THIS BUILDING IN EXISTENCE, NOT ITS BUILD DATE, and the record does not claim otherwise: on 31 March 1831 Jonathan N. Bailey was appointed postmaster and 'opened the post-office in a log house occupied as a store by John Stephen Coates' Hogan' (Andreas). The building was therefore already standing and already a store on that date, and nothing reached says when it went up — Hogan came to Chicago 'as early as 1830'. THE END OF THE RANGE IS THE HONEST MINIMUM AND IT IS THE WEAKEST THING IN THIS RECORD. What is attested is that the building stood and held the post office from March 1831 until about July 1834, when Andreas has the office removed to Franklin and South Water; that is eleven months before the scene date, and NO SOURCE REACHED FOLLOWS THE BUILDING PAST IT. The range is closed at the end of 1835 on the ordinary continuity argument — a standing building stands until something says otherwise, and this project's data/exclusions.json is where documented removals go — but the counter-argument is real and belongs here rather than in a footnote: Lake and South Water was the corner most exposed to the 1835 boom, log buildings on prime frontage were exactly what got replaced first, and the post office's own move out of it in July 1834 is unexplained. Tagged inferred, not documented, for that reason. If evidence turns up that this building came down before July 1835 it belongs in exclusions.json and this record leaves the scene.

position.symbolic_location: South bank of the main stem at the west end of the Lake Street / South Water Street block, near where the two streets converge east of Market Street; the north side of Lake Street, diagonally across it from the Sauganash.

derivation.note: The one placement here whose sources give a junction rather than a corner, so it carries the only non-zero offset in the dataset: 5 m east of Market Street's kerb, one narrow lot in from the corner rather than hard against it, because both sources say NEAR and ABOUT. That 5 m is an invention of position within a documented junction and it is now a number in the data instead of a phrase in a paragraph.

position.note: PLACED 2026-08-10. THE SOURCES AGREE ON A JUNCTION AND NEITHER GIVES A CORNER. Andreas, twice: 'near the present corner of Lake and South Water streets' and 'a small log building near the corner of Lake and South Water streets'. Currey: 'about where South Water street intersects Lake street, near the east end of the bridge'. Both say NEAR and ABOUT, and neither names a side of either street, so this coordinate is a placement inside a named junction rather than a corner lot read off a plat — which is the opposite of the Sauganash's and the Green Tree's positions, where the corner is documented and only the metres are derived. WHERE THAT JUNCTION IS: Lake Street and South Water Street run parallel through the town and meet only at their west ends, where the main stem turns south into the south branch and the block between them narrows to a wedge against Market Street. Currey's 'east end of the bridge' is the Lake Street raft bridge over the south branch and puts the same site at the same place. Method: the modern Lake Street / Market Street intersection centre (Market is today's N Wacker Drive) was read from OpenStreetMap at EPSG:26916 E 447161.9, N 4637285.4 — the same node this project used for the Sauganash — giving Lake Street's north kerb 12.2 m north of it and Market Street's east kerb 12.2 m east of it, half an 80 ft platted street in each direction. The footprint's south face is set on that Lake Street frontage and its west end about 5 m east of the Market kerb, one narrow lot in from the corner rather than hard against it, because both sources say near and about. NOTE A DISAGREEMENT THE OFFSET RESTS ON: this project's placement offsets use the 80 ft street width annotated on Hathaway 1834, and the Currey page states the Thompson 1830 plat laid out streets 'uniformly 66 feet wide'. The difference is 2.1 m in each offset, an order of magnitude inside the georeference's own error, so it does not move this building — but it is the first time the two figures have been seen to disagree in this dataset and it is recorded here and in docs/RESEARCH/hogan_store.md § 5 rather than being quietly averaged. UNCERTAINTY: about 20 m from the georeference, plus an unquantified allowance for 'near', which is the larger of the two here — the wedge block this building sits in is roughly 40 m of frontage before the ground runs out at the water. Facade bearing 180, due south onto Lake Street, and it is INFERRED FROM THE STREET RATHER THAN FROM ANY STATEMENT: nothing says which way this building faced, and a store fronting South Water and the river instead would rotate it 180 degrees and put its back to Lake. The choice also decides which of the building's two documented dimensions runs along the street — the 45 ft is set along Lake, because a store's long elevation is its frontage — and that assignment is inference, not evidence, even though both numbers are.

footprint.note: THE FIRST BUILDING FOOTPRINT IN THIS DATASET THAT IS NOT A PLACEHOLDER. Andreas gives the size twice, in two independently written passages: 'The building was twenty by forty-five feet in size, was partitioned off so as to serve as a post-office on one side, and as the store of Brewster, Hogan & Co., on the other', and, in the postmaster chronology, 'the store only occupied an area of forty-five by twenty feet'. 45 x 20 ft is 13.716 x 6.096 m, recorded here converted with the original figures stated, per data/datum.json's units rule. WHAT IS DOCUMENTED IS THE SIZE AND NOT THE PLAN: 'twenty by forty-five feet' is a rectangle in any reading, and this polygon is that rectangle, but nothing attests a door, a partition line on the ground, or that the building was exactly rectangular rather than a rectangle with something small attached. WHICH AXIS RUNS ALONG THE STREET IS NOT IN THE SOURCE either; it is decided by the facade bearing and argued in the position note, where it belongs, because rotating the building is what changes it. The 20 ft depth is worth reading twice: this is a 6 m deep building 13.7 m long, partitioned into a post office and a store, which is why Andreas offers it as evidence of 'the limited accommodations that were ample for the post-office of those days'.

construction.note: Three statements, two of them in Andreas: 'a log house occupied as a store by John Stephen Coates' Hogan', 'a small log building near the corner of Lake and South Water streets', and Currey's 'a log building about where South Water street intersects Lake street'. No source describes the corner treatment, the chinking or whether any of it was sided; the archetype builds hewn log, which is the commonest construction at the forks in 1835 and what all three descriptions name.

stories.note: Not stated. Andreas calls it 'a small log building' and gives it a 20 ft depth, and the two passages describing its use divide it side by side — a post office on one side and a store on the other — rather than by floor. A single-pen log building of this depth is single-storey by type at the forks in 1835. Inference from the type and the description, not from a statement.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.5 m is about 8 ft: one storey of hewn log wall at typical period course counts, plus a sill. What is inferred is that the wall height falls in this range, not that it is exactly 2.5 m — the same reading, and the same number, this project gives the Walker meeting house, which is the other single-storey log building it models.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for log construction of this type, period and region, and it is the form a 45 ft building of this depth is roofed with unless something says otherwise.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 35 degrees is the archetype's mid-range for a low single-storey log building roofed in riven shakes. Inferred from construction practice, not measured.

chimneys.note: Not attested, and nothing describes a stack on this building at all. One is the minimum for a store kept through Chicago winters with a clerk sorting mail in half of it, and the normal number for a single-pen log building. The COUNT is the inference; where the stack stands, how big it is and what it is made of are the archetype's, which is the standing admission in docs/LIBERTIES.md L26.

phases.change_note: The log store standing at the west end of the Lake Street block when the United States established a post office at Chicago on 31 March 1831, and for three years the building that held it: partitioned into a post office on one side and the store of Brewster, Hogan & Co. on the other, with John Bates Jr. sorting the mail from 1833. The post office moved out to Franklin and South Water about July 1834; that is a change of USE and does not open a new phase, and it is why this building is not the post office on the scene date.

function.note: NOT THE POST OFFICE AT THE SCENE DATE, which is the fact this record exists to get right. It held Chicago's first post office from 31 March 1831 until about July 1834, when Andreas has the office removed to near the corner of Franklin and South Water, where it stayed through Hogan's term. What the building was doing on 1835-07-01 is NOT ATTESTED: it is recorded as a store because that is what it was before the post office arrived ('a log house occupied as a store') and alongside it for three years, and because nothing describes it changing to anything else. Brewster, Hogan & Co. advertised as forwarding and commission merchants in the early numbers of the Chicago Democrat, but no source reached puts the firm in THIS building in 1835, so the record carries no occupants block rather than guessing at one.

research_note: THE BUILDING WHERE CHICAGO'S MAIL BEGAN, and the first record in this dataset whose footprint is evidence rather than a placeholder: Andreas states its size twice, twenty by forty-five feet, as an aside about how little room the town's post office needed. Everything else about it is thin — no build date, no orientation, no description beyond 'small' and 'log', and no source follows it past 1834. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THIS PROJECT'S OWN DOSSIER CAME OUT OF WRITING IT, both in docs/research/03-structures-north.md § 4, and both because a page was opened that the dossier's table had only summarised. First, the dossier dates the move to the Franklin and South Water office from 2 November 1832, the day Hogan succeeded Bailey as postmaster; Andreas says twice that the office was still at Lake and South Water through 1833 and moved 'about July' 1834, so the 1832 date is the postmaster's, not the building's. Second, the dossier's own source for the 1832 date, the Currey page, is where that conflation comes from — it makes the appointment and the move one sentence — and it also gives the corner as 'south west', which Andreas never does. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE SCENE: on 1835-07-01 the post office is a DIFFERENT, UNMODELLED building near Franklin and South Water, about 100 m east of this one, and nothing reached describes its construction, its size or its side of either street. It is a candidate for a later slice and it would be almost entirely invention today; that is stated in docs/RESEARCH/hogan_store.md § 4 rather than being built. THE WEAK POINT OF THIS RECORD IS ITS SURVIVAL, not its geometry: it is attested standing to about July 1834 and placed in a scene set eleven months later on a continuity argument, which is set out in full on documented_range. See docs/RESEARCH/hogan_store.md.
